claim: Metformin is a widely used first-line drug for treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D).
source: Metformin, a widely used first-line drug for treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D), has been shown to extend lifespan and delay the onset of age-related diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about metformin's clinical use.

claim: Metformin has been shown to extend lifespan and delay the onset of age-related diseases.
source: Metformin, a widely used first-line drug for treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D), has been shown to extend lifespan and delay the onset of age-related diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing multiple studies.

claim: Metformin acts through the v-ATPase-Ragulator lysosomal pathway to coordinate mTORC1 and AMPK.
source: Using a pure in vitro reconstitution system, we demonstrate that metformin acts through the v-ATPase-Ragulator lysosomal pathway to coordinate mTORC1 and AMPK, two hubs governing metabolic programs.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both v-ATPase-mediated TORC1 inhibition and v-ATPase-AXIN/LKB1-mediated AMPK activation contribute to the lifespan extension effect of metformin in C. elegans.
source: We further show in Caenorhabditis elegans that both v-ATPase-mediated TORC1 inhibition and v-ATPase-AXIN/LKB1-mediated AMPK activation contribute to the lifespan extension effect of metformin.
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments in C. elegans shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: Administration of metformin has been shown to extend lifespan in C. elegans and mice.
source: Administration of metformin, a first-line drug for treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D), has been shown to extend lifespan in C. elegans and mice (Anisimov et al., 2008; Cabreiro et al., 2013; De Haes et al., 2014; Martin-Montalvo et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Metformin has been shown to ameliorate diabetic and cardiovascular diseases in patients.
source: In addition, metformin has been shown to ameliorate diabetic and cardiovascular diseases in patients (Scarpello, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Metformin lowered the incidence of several age-related diseases, such as cancer, metabolic syndrome and cognitive disorders.
source: Metformin also lowered the incidence of several other age-related diseases, such as cancer, metabolic syndrome and cognitive disorders (Foretz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A clinical trial named TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) was proposed to evaluate metformin's protective effects against human aging and age-related diseases.
source: Due to its broad range of health benefits and little side effects, a clinical trial named TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) was proposed to evaluate metformin's protective effects against human aging and age-related diseases (Barzilai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published proposal.

claim: Metformin is generally believed to act through activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
source: Metformin is generally believed to act through activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Fryer et al., 2002; Hawley et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2001), a principal energy sensor that when activated, switches on catabolic pathways such as glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation to produce more ATP (Burkewitz et al., 2014; Hardie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: AMPK is a principal energy sensor that when activated, switches on catabolic pathways such as glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation to produce more ATP.
source: Metformin is generally believed to act through activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Fryer et al., 2002; Hawley et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2001), a principal energy sensor that when activated, switches on catabolic pathways such as glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation to produce more ATP (Burkewitz et al., 2014; Hardie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies describing AMPK function.

claim: It was proposed that metformin might act through inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) Complex I.
source: It was proposed that metformin might act through inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) Complex I (El-Mir et al., 2000; Foretz et al., 2014; Owen et al., 2000), resulting in a change of the AMP/ATP ratio and ultimately activating AMPK.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies proposing this mechanism.

claim: The idea that metformin acts through inhibition of mitochondrial ETC Complex I has been challenged recently.
source: However, this idea has been challenged recently (He and Wondisford, 2015), especially when physiological/low concentration (~70 uM) of metformin, which cannot induce AMP/ATP change, is still able to activate AMPK (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies challenging the Complex I mechanism.

claim: Physiological/low concentration (~70 uM) of metformin, which cannot induce AMP/ATP change, is still able to activate AMPK.
source: However, this idea has been challenged recently (He and Wondisford, 2015), especially when physiological/low concentration (~70 uM) of metformin, which cannot induce AMP/ATP change, is still able to activate AMPK (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: An alternative model proposes that metformin activates AMPK through the lysosome-dependent pathway.
source: An alternative model, in which metformin activates AMPK through the lysosome-dependent pathway was proposed (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Metformin treatment induces lysosomal localization of the scaffold protein AXIN.
source: In this model, metformin treatment induces lysosomal localization of the scaffold protein AXIN, which brings its associated protein liver kinase B1 (LKB1) to form a complex with v-ATPase-Ragulator on the surface of lysosome (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: LKB1 phosphorylates the threonine residue in the activation loop of AMPK, leading to AMPK activation.
source: LKB1 then phosphorylates the threonine residue in the activation loop of AMPK, leading to AMPK activation (Hawley et al., 1996; Shaw et al., 2004; Woods et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Metformin administration inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1).
source: In addition to AMPK activation, metformin administration also inhibit mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) (Kalender et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: mTORC1 constitutes a hub for energy and nutrient sensing, and switches on anabolism when activated.
source: mTORC1 constitutes another hub for energy and nutrient sensing, and switches on anabolism when activated (Schmelzle and Hall, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study and represents established knowledge.

claim: The primary pathway for mTORC1 activation requires lysosome-localized Rag GTPases, which form RagA/B–RagC/D heterodimers.
source: The primary pathway for mTORC1 activation requires lysosome-localized Rag GTPases, which form RagA/B–RagC/D heterodimers and recruit mTORC1 to the surface of lysosome through directly binding to the Raptor subunit of mTORC1 (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: v-ATPase-Ragulator complex on lysosomal surface is required for the spatial regulation and activation of mTORC1 by Rag GTPases.
source: v-ATPase-Ragulator complex on lysosomal surface is required for the spatial regulation and activation of mTORC1 by Rag GTPases (Bar-Peled et al., 2012; Dibble and Manning, 2013; Jewell et al., 2013; Sancak et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Two distinct mechanisms have been proposed for metformin-induced mTORC1 inhibition: suppression of Rag GTPases (AMPK-independent mechanism) or AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor (AMPK-dependent mechanism).
source: Two distinct mechanisms have been proposed for metformin-induced mTORC1 inhibition: suppression of Rag GTPases (AMPK-independent mechanism) or AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor (regulatory associated protein of mTORC1) (AMPK-dependent mechanism) (Howell et al., 2017; Kalender et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: C. elegans is a powerful model organism to test the efficacy of metformin in promoting healthspan due to its short lifespan and ease of genetic manipulation.
source: Due to its short lifespan and ease of genetic manipulation, C. elegans becomes a powerful model organism to test the efficacy of metformin in promoting healthspan (Burkewitz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: Metformin treatment greatly extends worm lifespan and improves fitness, for example prolonging locomotory ability.
source: It has been shown that metformin treatment greatly extends worm lifespan and improves fitness, for example prolonging locomotory ability (Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Metformin administration may mimic a dietary restriction (DR) metabolism in C. elegans.
source: For instance, metformin administration may mimic a dietary restriction (DR) metabolism (Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Alteration of methionine metabolism in C. elegans has been shown to play a partial role in metformin's effects.
source: In addition, alteration of methionine metabolism in C. elegans has been shown to play a partial role (Cabreiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Metformin has been shown to inhibit mTORC1 due to restricted transit of RagA-RagC GTPase through nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: Recently, metformin has been shown to inhibit mTORC1 due to restricted transit of RagA-RagC GTPase through nuclear pore complex (NPC) (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: mTORC1 and AMPK share the common activator, v-ATPase-Ragulator complex.
source: Intrigued by the discoveries that mTORC1 and AMPK share the common activator, v-ATPase-Ragulator complex (Zhang et al., 2014), and that metformin may directly act on the lysosomal pathway to promote AMPK activation (Zhang et al., 2016), we sought to set up a pure in vitro reconstitution system to explore the mechanism of metformin's action (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Upon amino acids stimulation, significant portion of Raptor accumulated on the lysosome, indicating the activation of mTORC1 pathway.
source: Upon amino acids stimulation, significant portion of Raptor accumulated on the lysosome (Figure 1C,F), indicating the activation of mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1F.

claim: Addition of Concanavalin A (Con A) or metformin dissociated Raptor from the lysosome.
source: Addition of Con A or metformin dissociated Raptor from the lysosome (Figure 1D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1G.

claim: Metformin's effect on mTORC1 inhibition does not require AMPK.
source: To test if metformin's effect on mTORC1 inhibition requires AMPK or not, we repeated the in vitro experiments in AMPK knockout MEF cells, and still observed the dissociation of Raptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metformin inhibits mTORC1 through the lysosomal pathway independent of AMPK, possibly mimicking Con A to inhibit v-ATPase.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that metformin inhibits mTORC1 through the lysosomal pathway independent of AMPK, possibly mimicking Con A to inhibit v-ATPase.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AXIN/LKB1 were recruited to metformin- or Con A-treated lysosomes, and were sufficient to phosphorylate endogenous AMPK in an amino acid-independent manner.
source: Consistent with previous findings, AXIN/LKB1 were recruited to metformin- or Con A-treated lysosomes, and were sufficient to phosphorylate endogenous AMPK in an amino acid-independent manner (Figure 1E,H) (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1H, and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: Unlike rotenone, metformin treatment showed no mitochondrial stress response reporter activation in C. elegans hsp-6p::gfp reporter strain.
source: Unlike rotenone, metformin treatment showed no reporter activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Metformin administration impaired lysosomal function as measured by cathepsin assay.
source: Consistent with our idea, metformin administration indeed impaired lysosomal function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claim: Metformin treatment significantly decreased the level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation in C. elegans.
source: Notably, metformin treatment significantly decreased the level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation (Figure 2A,B), suggesting an inhibition of TORC1 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: HLH-30 translocalized to the nucleus in the tail region of C. elegans upon metformin administration.
source: Indeed, HLH-30 translocalized to the nucleus in the tail region of C. elegans upon metformin administration (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: HLH-30 is an ortholog of transcription factor EB (TFEB) that translocates to the nucleus upon TORC1 inhibition.
source: We also tested the subcellular localization of HLH-30, an ortholog of transcription factor EB (TFEB) that translocates to the nucleus upon TORC1 inhibition (Lapierre et al., 2013; Perera and Zoncu, 2016; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Once in the nucleus, HLH-30 regulates the transcription of genes related to autophagy, lysosome function and lipid hydrolysis.
source: Once in the nucleus, HLH-30 regulates the transcription of genes related to autophagy, lysosome function and lipid hydrolysis (Lapierre et al., 2013; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Up-regulation of transcript levels of hlh-30 downstream targets was observed upon metformin treatment.
source: Consistently, we also observed up-regulation of transcript levels of hlh-30 downstream targets upon metformin treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Metformin inhibits TORC1 pathway in C. elegans.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that metformin inhibits TORC1 pathway in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Metformin treatment of aak-2 loss-of-function mutants was still able to drive HLH-30 nuclear accumulation.
source: Consistent with our results in AMPK-/- MEF cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), metformin treatment of aak-2 (Ce.AMPK) loss-of-function mutants was still able to drive HLH-30 nuclear accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) and elevate the expression of HLH-30 target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: Inhibition of TORC1 has been shown to result in lifespan extension.
source: Inhibition of TORC1 has been shown to result in lifespan extension (Jia et al., 2004; Vellai et al., 2003); also reviewed by Zoncu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: daf-15 heterozygous mutants had a longer lifespan and a decreased level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation compared with control worms.
source: Compared with the control worms, daf-15 heterozygous mutants had a longer lifespan and a decreased level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that TORC1 inhibition extends C. elegans lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Metformin treatment greatly extended the lifespan of daf-15 heterozygous mutants.
source: More importantly, metformin treatment greatly extended the lifespan of daf-15 heterozygous mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metformin administration decreased neutral fat level in daf-15 heterozygous mutants similar to wild type animals.
source: Similar to wild type animals, metformin administration further decreased neutral fat level in daf-15 heterozygous mutants (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Metformin treatment significantly increased the locomotory ability and reduced age pigments of wild type worms and daf-15 heterozygous mutants.
source: Metformin treatment significantly increased the locomotory ability (counted by the average bends of worm body per 60 s) and reduced age pigments of wild type worms and daf-15 heterozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and Figure 3D,E), indicating that metformin also improves fitness of daf-15 heterozygous mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: In daf-15 heterozygous mutants, significant portion of HLH-30 already localized in the nucleus, suggesting an inhibition of TORC1 activity.
source: We found that in daf-15 heterozygous mutants, significant portion of HLH-30 already localized in the nucleus, suggesting an inhibition of TORC1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Metformin administration increased HLH-30 nuclear localization in control worms, but not in daf-15 heterozygous mutants.
source: More importantly, metformin administration increased HLH-30 nuclear localization in control worms, but not in daf-15 heterozygous mutants (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Metformin could still extend lifespans of hlh-30, pha-4 or skn-1 mutants.
source: We found that metformin could still extend lifespans of hlh-30, pha-4 or skn-1 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Metformin activated AMPK in daf-15 heterozygous mutant to the same level as that in the control worms.
source: Given that metformin activated AMPK in daf-15 heterozygous mutant to the same level as that in the control worms (Figure 3H,I), it is likely that metformin promotes longevity also through activation of AMPK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and 3I.

claim: Metformin may act on a pathway additive to that of TORC1 inhibition to confer fitness benefit.
source: These results suggest that metformin may act on a pathway additive to that of TORC1 inhibition to confer fitness benefit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing metformin's effects in daf-15 heterozygous mutants.

claim: vha-3 and vha-12 mutants had longer lifespans compared with wild type animals.
source: vha-3 and vha-12 mutants had longer lifespans compared with wild type animals, whereas lifespan of lmtr-2 or lmtr-3 mutants was comparable to that of the wild type animals (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: Lifespan of lmtr-2 or lmtr-3 mutants was comparable to that of the wild type animals.
source: vha-3 and vha-12 mutants had longer lifespans compared with wild type animals, whereas lifespan of lmtr-2 or lmtr-3 mutants was comparable to that of the wild type animals (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: RNAi knockdown of vha-3 but not lmtr-3, was sufficient to induce the nuclear accumulation of HLH-30 and activate HLH-30 downstream targets.
source: Indeed, RNAi knockdown of vha-3 but not lmtr-3, was sufficient to induce the nuclear accumulation of HLH-30 and activate HLH-30 downstream targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C and D, and Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C and 4D.

claim: Knocking down of vha-3 but not lmtr-3, decreased the level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation.
source: In addition, knocking down of vha-3 but not lmtr-3, decreased the level of RSKS-1 phosphorylation (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Metformin administration could not further induce the lifespan extension, nor AAK-2 activation in v-ATPase mutants vha-3 and vha-12, or Ragulator mutants lmtr-3 and lmtr-2.
source: More importantly, metformin administration could not further induce the lifespan extension, nor AAK-2 activation in v-ATPase mutants vha-3 and vha-12, or Ragulator mutants lmtr-3 and lmtr-2 (Figure 4B–C and I–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, B, E and F), suggesting that metformin's effect on lifespan extension may also depend on the lysosomal pathway of AMPK activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, 4I, 4J, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, 4B, 4E, and 4F.

claim: Metformin's effect on lifespan extension may depend on the lysosomal pathway of AMPK activation.
source: More importantly, metformin administration could not further induce the lifespan extension, nor AAK-2 activation in v-ATPase mutants vha-3 and vha-12, or Ragulator mutants lmtr-3 and lmtr-2 (Figure 4B–C and I–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, B, E and F), suggesting that metformin's effect on lifespan extension may also depend on the lysosomal pathway of AMPK activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing metformin's effects in v-ATPase and Ragulator mutants.

claim: Metformin shortens the lifespan of lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 mutants.
source: It should be noted that metformin even shortens the lifespan of lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 mutants (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Fractions of censored animals were not increased in metformin-treated lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 mutants.
source: However, fractions of censored animals were not increased in metformin-treated lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 4G), suggesting that metformin did not make the mutants sick.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4G.

claim: AXIN is a scaffold protein required for lysosomal localization of LKB1 and lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK.
source: AXIN is a scaffold protein required for lysosomal localization of LKB1 and lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: AXL-1 only localized on the lysosome upon metformin treatment in mammalian cells.
source: Therefore, we expressed EGFP-tagged AXL-1 in mammalian cells and showed that AXL-1 only localized on the lysosome upon metformin treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Without metformin administration, axl-1 mutant alone did not perturb lysosomal function.
source: Consistently, without metformin administration, axl-1 mutant alone did not perturb lysosomal function (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Metformin treatment failed to activate AAK-2 in axl-1 mutant.
source: Metformin treatment failed to activate AAK-2 (Ce.AMPK) in axl-1 mutant (AXIN-deficient animals) (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Metformin was not able to extend lifespan of axl-1 mutant animals.
source: Consistently, metformin was no longer able to extend lifespan of axl-1 mutant animals (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Metformin could not extend lifespan of par-4 mutants.
source: Similar to axl-1, metformin could not extend lifespan of par-4 (C. elegans ortholog of LKB-1) mutants as well (Figure 5F) (Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and a citation to a published study.

claim: v-ATPase-Ragulator-AXIN-LKB1-based lysosome pathway is required for the metformin's effects of lifespan extension.
source: Taken together, these genetic evidences indicate that v-ATPase-Ragulator-AXIN-LKB1-based lysosome pathway is required for the metformin's effects of lifespan extension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Metformin has been shown to trigger a dietary restriction-like state and extend C. elegans lifespan through AMPK pathway.
source: It has been shown that metformin triggers a dietary restriction-like state and extends C. elegans lifespan through AMPK pathway (Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Metformin administration induced a dietary restriction-like state to decrease neutral fat level in wild type animals.
source: Indeed, metformin administration induced a dietary restriction-like state to decrease neutral fat level in wild type animals (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: vha-3, lmtr-3 and axl-1 mutants retained the same levels of ORO staining in the presence or absence of metformin.
source: Conversely, vha-3 (v-ATPase V0), lmtr-3 (Ragulator) and axl-1 (AXIN) mutants retained the same levels of ORO staining in the presence or absence of metformin (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that the dietary restriction-like state triggered by metformin requires the lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The dietary restriction-like state triggered by metformin requires the lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK.
source: Conversely, vha-3 (v-ATPase V0), lmtr-3 (Ragulator) and axl-1 (AXIN) mutants retained the same levels of ORO staining in the presence or absence of metformin (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that the dietary restriction-like state triggered by metformin requires the lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing metformin's effects on neutral fat levels in various mutants.

claim: Mutation of vha-3, lmtr-3 or axl-1 impaired metformin's effects on locomotion and age pigments.
source: Strikingly, mutation of vha-3, lmtr-3 or axl-1 impaired metformin's effects on locomotion and age pigments (Figure 6D–G), suggesting that lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK is also required for metformin-attenuated fitness decline in aged animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D, 6E, 6F, and 6G.

claim: Lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK is required for metformin-attenuated fitness decline in aged animals.
source: Strikingly, mutation of vha-3, lmtr-3 or axl-1 impaired metformin's effects on locomotion and age pigments (Figure 6D–G), suggesting that lysosome-dependent activation of AMPK is also required for metformin-attenuated fitness decline in aged animals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing metformin's effects on locomotion and age pigments in various mutants.

claim: Using a pure in vitro reconstitution system that excludes mitochondria, metformin coordinates mTORC1 inhibition and AMPK activation through lysosomal pathway.
source: Using a pure in vitro reconstitution system that excludes mitochondria, we showed that metformin coordinates mTORC1 inhibition and AMPK activation through lysosomal pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Metformin extends C. elegans lifespan and attenuates age-related fitness decline via a mechanism that requires v-ATPase-Ragulator-AXIN/LKB1 of the lysosomal pathway.
source: We further employed genetic manipulation to show that metformin extends C. elegans lifespan and attenuates age-related fitness decline via similar mechanism that requires v-ATPase-Ragulator-AXIN/LKB1 of the lysosomal pathway (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: Metformin may function by targeting and priming v-ATPase-Ragulator complex on lysosome membrane, which serves as a hub to coordinate mTORC1 and AMPK pathways and govern metabolic programs.
source: Metformin may function by targeting and priming v-ATPase-Ragulator complex on lysosome membrane, which serves as a hub to coordinate mTORC1 and AMPK pathways and govern metabolic programs.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Metformin administration might result in a conformational change of v-ATPase-Ragulator complex, which dissociates mTORC1 from lysosome and allows the docking of AXIN/LKB1 for AMPK activation.
source: It is possible that metformin administration might result in a conformational change of v-ATPase-Ragulator complex, which dissociates mTORC1 from lysosome and allows the docking of AXIN/LKB1 for AMPK activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is a speculative model based on the experimental results.

claim: The purity of lysosome preparation was confirmed by immunoblotting to test for the absence of early endosome, mitochondria, ER or nuclei.
source: The purity of lysosome preparation was confirmed by immunoblotting to test for the absence of early endosome, mitochondria, ER or nuclei (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Immuno-purified LKB1 forms a complex with endogenous STRAD and MO25, two proteins essential for optimal LKB1 activity.
source: Immuno-purified LKB1 forms a complex with endogenous STRAD and MO25, two proteins essential for optimal LKB1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: T389 of S6K1 is highly conserved among species.
source: We used an antibody that specifically detects Thr-389, a highly conserved phosphorylation site among species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VHA-3, VHA-12, LMTR-3 and LMTR-12 all localized on the lysosomes of C. elegans.
source: VHA-3, VHA-12, LMTR-3 and LMTR-12 all localized on the lysosomes of C. elegans, as they have similar staining pattern with lysosomal marker LMP-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: All vha-3, vha-12, lmtr-3, and lmtr-2 mutants had impaired lysosomes, which could be rescued with the expression of corresponding gene.
source: All these four mutants had impaired lysosomes, which could be rescued with the expression of corresponding gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lifespan extension in vha-3 and vha-12 mutants might be due to Ce.TOR inhibition, because v-ATPase is required for the spatial regulation and subsequent activation of TORC1.
source: Lifespan extension in vha-3 and vha-12 mutants might be due to Ce.TOR inhibition, because v-ATPase is required for the spatial regulation and subsequent activation of TORC1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and established knowledge about v-ATPase function.

claim: Failure of lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 to induce lifespan extension suggested that Ce.TOR pathway was not inhibited under lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 deficiency.
source: Consistently, failure of lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 to induce lifespan extension suggested that Ce.TOR pathway was not inhibited under lmtr-3 or lmtr-2 deficiency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing no lifespan extension in lmtr mutants.
